title: Christ and culture
hookLine: some Christians set themselves apart, some work to change the culture, some live in two kingdoms at once
carry: in the world, not of it

lines: A PRAYER ON THE LAST NIGHT.
IN THE WORLD. NOT OF THE WORLD.
cards: It's the night before Jesus dies, and in John 17 he prays aloud for his friends. A few verses apart, he says two things about them. "These are in the world," he says.
And then: "They are not of the world." Some Christians fold the pair into one short saying: in the world, not of it. Both halves stand.
Nobody is taken out, and nobody simply blends in. So how do you live inside that pair of sentences? Christians have worked out different answers.

teach.h: NOT OUT OF THE WORLD, BUT KEPT.
teach.b: Here's the heart of Jesus' prayer: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil." Not out. Kept.
So the question becomes how. The theologian H. Richard Niebuhr wrote a book called Christ and Culture that sorted Christian answers into types.
Three of them are easy to spot.

Some Christians set themselves apart. Amish and other Anabaptist communities, and monks and nuns in their own way, draw clear lines between their life and the wider culture, so they can live differently together.
They point to Paul: "be not conformed to this world." Some Christians aim to change the culture from inside: in schools, hospitals, laws, art, business.

teach.h: CHANGE IT: THE SALT OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: They point to Jesus: "Ye are the salt of the earth." Salt doesn't leave the food. It changes the taste.
And some live in two kingdoms at once. Martin Luther taught that God governs in two ways, through the gospel and through the law and sword of rulers, and a Christian lives under both.
Christians in this line point to Jesus, asked about paying taxes: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."
Each has its scriptures, its saints and its honest arguments, and this path won't rank them.
A single life can hold some of all three: a line you won't cross, a place where you're trying to be salt, and two sets of duties you carry at once.

how: Christians live this out in different ways: some in communities that keep apart from the wider culture, some through work in public life, schools and the arts, and some by teaching two kingdoms, with duties to both church and state.

practice: Walk through the places you'll be in the next few days, work, home, a screen, a store, maybe a church, and in each one ask quietly: where do I blend in here, and where do I live a little differently?
Don't grade the answers; just notice. If you pray, you can hold those places before God one by one.

orig.note: Greek: world; in John's Gospel it can mean the world God loves (John 3:16) and the world that resists him.
